title: friction-signal-workbench-annotated-deltas-2026-01-30
content:
Purpose:
Runbook-style working notes synthesizing the last 6 weeks of frontline customer reports, small-request patterns, and lightweight feature asks. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: focus on low-effort probes that reduce friction customers hit when using hosted inference and Dedicated pools.

Context summary (topline):
- Recurring theme: unpredictable latency spikes for short-chat workloads and tokenized preview requests (customers see 95th percentile blowouts during cold KV cache misses).
- Secondary: asks to make fallbacks more explicit in SDKs (customers want a programmatic way to know when a cheaper / lower-latency model was used as a fallback).
- Tertiary: enterprise customers request safer diagnostic metadata exposure (sampled traces, not full data).

Representative customer notes (raw excerpts):
- "We serve autocompletes and a few-shot summarizer; sometimes users wait 1.2s, other times 80ms. Hard to justify an SLA to product managers." — fintech startup, applied to hosted-api
- "Our billing spikes correlate with repeated long context reruns; maybe cache TTL is too short for our traffic pattern." — analytics vendor on Dedicated
- "SDK hid fallback to smaller model; we lost fidelity and couldn't detect it automatically." — marketplace team

Observed signal patterns (metrics hooks):
- Cold-cache tail: 1.5–2x token latency increase when kv-cache miss > 150ms; happens most on requests with small prompt sizes (<=120 tokens) and high QPS bursts.
- Batching interplay: enabling larger batch windows reduces cost but increases observed 95th latency for interactive flows.
- Fallbacks active: ~1.3% of requests for some mid-market tenants over last 30d used model-variant fallback during peak time windows.

Hypothesis bank (ranked):
1) Cache TTL mismatch: default TTL optimized for long-run generation workloads, not interactive short prompts — short prompts thrash the cache.
2) Heuristic routing opacity: customers can’t observe when a request is routed off their pinned Dedicated pool to a compatible shared variant; they assume degradation or billing mismatch.
3) SDK ergonomics: no single callback surface for fallback/route metadata, so app teams bake brittle heuristics.

Low-effort probes (<= 5 engineer-days):
- Probe A: "sticky-prefix" experiment — increase default KV cache TTL for keys under 200 tokens for a 7-day window on a small set of tenants (A/B).
  - Owner: Marco Chen
  - Success metric: 95th latency down by >= 20% on interactive endpoints, no >2% cost delta.
  - Risk: cache memory pressure; mitigation: cap by tenant and evict LRU first.

- Probe B: "fallback flag" SDK patch (JS + Python) — include an opt-in request-level header and SDK hook (onFallback) that surfaces when platform routes to a variant model or a different capacity tier.
  - Owner: Lena Ortiz
  - Success metric: adoption by 5 customers + reduced support tickets about silent fidelity drops.
  - Risk: surface could be abused; mitigation: opt-in and rate-limited samples.

- Probe C: "trace-sampler" privacy-safe diagnostic — sampled trace with redaction rules (headers + token prefixes removed) to share with customers under NDA during incident triage.
  - Owner: Samir Rao
  - Success metric: reduction in time-to-resolve (TTR) for incidents by 30% for participating customers.
  - Risk: privacy leak; mitigation: strict redaction + legal signoff.

Proposed medium-effort projects (2–4 sprints):
- Feature: Cost/Quality incident dashboard (per-tenant) that shows fallbacks, model-variant use, and per-route token economics. Would require data pipeline changes and UI. Estimate: infra 3s, backend 3s, frontend 2s.
- Feature: Dedicated pool routing transparency — customers can set a strict/soft mode for routing fallbacks. Strict mode guarantees no fallbacks but permits request rejection; soft mode auto-fallbacks to maintain availability. Estimate: infra 4s, policy + docs 1s.

Open questions and unknowns (notes-to-self):
- Do we have telemetry to tie a specific fallback to the exact model variant version? (Action: SRE/telemetry to confirm)
- Memory/cost trade-offs for sticky-prefix TTLs — need cache-eviction simulations on 6 tenant traces.
- Legal: what minimal trace syntax is acceptable for customers in regulated industries? (Action: loop in legal and security)

Immediate next steps (1–2 weeks):
1) Run sticky-prefix TTL A/B on 8 low-risk tenants — Marco to deploy test config and collect latency/cost delta. Deadline: 2026-01-22 (in flight).
2) Ship fallback-flag SDK PR (alpha) to internal dogfood customers — Lena to cut PR and add test harness. Deadline: 2026-01-28.
3) Draft trace redaction policy + sample payload — Samir to sync with Security. Deadline: 2026-01-25.
4) Triage Linear issues tagged INF-842 and link results here.

Decision log (short):
- 2026-01-16: agreed to prioritize low-effort probes first.
- 2026-01-20: restrict sticky-prefix to tenants with <5GB cache footprint.

Slack / Tickets to reference:
- Slack thread: C02KJ4X9T (customer-reports)
- Linear: INF-842, INF-911 (sdk-fallback-flag), INF-918 (trace-redaction)

Appendix: quick UX copy for fallback flag docs (for SDK README)
- "Opt-in header: X-Redwood-Fallback: true — When enabled, your application will receive a one-off event when the platform routes a request to a different model variant or capacity tier. Use for debugging and backfill validation. Sample usage: client.on('fallback', (info) => { log(info.model, info.reason) })"

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Keep experiments small. Customers want quick wins (latency and explainability) more than big dashboards right now.
- Capture a short customer-facing note for each probe; avoid engineering jargon — product will own the outward comms.

-- Aisha
